questions.stem: Describe the start of the universe according to the Big Bang theory.
questions.modelAnswer: Roughly 14 billion years have passed since the universe burst outward from a tiny region that was extremely hot and dense.

questions.stem: State what happens to the distances between galaxies as the universe expands.
questions.modelAnswer: The distances grow: each point moves away from the others as space stretches.

questions.stem: Explain why more distant galaxies recede faster in an expanding universe.
questions.modelAnswer: Expansion stretches the space between every pair of points, so the more space lies between two galaxies, the faster the gap grows — distant galaxies recede faster, just as far-apart balloon dots separate quickest.

questions.stem: Galaxy A sits twice as far from us as galaxy B. In the same expansion period, compare how far each galaxy's distance from us grows.
questions.modelAnswer: Galaxy A's distance grows by about twice as much as galaxy B's, because the stretch of space is proportional to the separation.

questions.stem: Name the two main pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
questions.modelAnswer: Two pillars: the red-shift of galaxies and the cosmic microwave background — the CMB.

questions.stem: State the wavelength region and approximate value of the CMB.
questions.modelAnswer: Microwaves, with a wavelength of around 1 mm.

questions.stem: Explain why the CMB supports the Big Bang theory.
questions.modelAnswer: The early universe was extremely hot and dense, so it must have emitted thermal radiation; the expansion red-shifted that glow over 14 billion years into microwaves arriving uniformly from all directions — a profile exactly like a hot body that has cooled, which rival theories cannot explain.

questions.stem: A map of the CMB shows warm patches and cool patches differing by about 0.00001 K. State what the warm patches indicate.
questions.modelAnswer: The warmer regions mark a higher density of galaxies, stars and planets.
